cards.title: Define the Market by Job, Not Product or Customer Category
cards.summary: Re-framing the market around the customer's Job to Be Done reveals growth where product- or demographic-based categories show none.
cards.use_when: You are sizing a market, prioritizing a roadmap, or suspect your category definition is hiding demand (e.g., an ecommerce brand defining itself by product type instead of the progress customers want).
steps: List the product or customer categories your business currently uses to describe its market (e.g., 'mattresses', 'women 25-40').
For each, restate it as the progress a customer is trying to make in a circumstance (e.g., 'help me wake up without pain so I can be productive as a parent and worker').
Look at who solves that job today — including products in other categories, workarounds, and doing nothing — because those are your real competitors.

Re-estimate the market from this job perspective; the addressable set often looks very different. The book's example: P&G assumed low-cost diapers would sell to millions of non-diaper-using Chinese parents, but the functional 'containment device' framing missed the emotional/social job of a baby sleeping through the night.
caveats: Reframing does not guarantee a large market; the job must have enough magnitude to change behavior.
The Pampers China outcome (approx. $1.6B and ~30% share by 2013) is a reported case result, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Drill Deep and Look Wide: Functional, Emotional, Social Dimensions
cards.summary: A job has functional, emotional and social dimensions; innovations that only address the functional miss context and fail.
cards.use_when: You are defining requirements for a product, page, or experience and want to avoid the common trap of solving only the functional dimension.
steps: For a promising job, write out the functional dimension (what task it performs), the social dimension (how the customer wants to be seen by others), and the emotional dimension (how they want to feel).
Treat all three as potentially equal in weight; do not assume emotional/social are secondary to functional.

In the book's Intermountain example, clinicians were given state-of-the-art diagnostic software but chose paper and pen because typing broke eye contact during a diagnosis — the emotional job of reassuring an anxious patient beat the functional tool.
Audit your own offering the same way: what functional problem does it solve, and what emotional/social reassurance is either helped or harmed at that moment?
caveats: The source attributes the 'don't separate the three dimensions' insight to P&G's David Goulait; it is presented as his conversion, not a universal law.
Emotional/social weight varies by circumstance; don't assume it always dominates.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Don't Do Design Requirements in a Conference Room — Go Into the Wild
cards.summary: Asking experts what they want in a conference room misses the real job; observe people in the actual circumstances where they use the product.
cards.use_when: You are gathering requirements from internal stakeholders, power users, or customers via interviews and need to validate that stated needs match real behavior.
steps: Note the trap: asking people what they need and building exactly that, based on the assumption that they can explain their own job accurately.
Actually watch the product being used in its real context (the clinic, the kitchen, the checkout flow) before finalizing requirements.

Look for the gap between what people say they do and what they do — Intermountain found clinicians' stated needs didn't match what they actually wanted in practice, and they had missed a whole customer: the patient.
Maintain a 'beginner's mind'; the source's goal is to observe the job, not just catalog behavior sequence ('what happened first, second').
caveats: This is the source's opinion (voiced via Intermountain's Todd Dunn) that 'you can't do design requirements in a conference room.' Apply with judgment for your context.
For ecommerce, transfer the technique as observing real browsing/checkout behavior and customer support context rather than assuming stated preferences.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Study Nonconsumers and Workarounds for High-Potential Jobs
cards.summary: People who buy nothing (not even from competitors) and people inventing workarounds often reveal the richest unmet jobs.
cards.use_when: Your growth has plateaued with current customers and you want to find new demand outside your existing base.
steps: Identify nonconsumers: people who aren't buying your product or anyone else's for this job.
Ask what makes nonconsumers' jobs different from current customers' jobs, and what's blocking them from using any solution.
Watch for 'compensating behavior' — people rigging their own workaround. The source treats this as a strong clue that the job is important and the person is frustrated enough to invent a solution.
For ecommerce, look at searchers who bounce, abandoned carts, and people using spreadsheets/manual processes instead of buying a tool.
caveats: The book states most companies over-invest in studying current customers; nonconsumers are the underused source, not a replacement.
Workarounds signal opportunity but not guaranteed willingness to switch.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
cards.summary: Most data tracks the purchase (Big Hire) but ignores the moment of consumption (Little Hire), which determines whether the product really solves the job.
cards.use_when: You are measuring product-market fit, retention, or why downloads/purchases don't translate into repeat use.
steps: Define the Big Hire: the purchase moment (e.g., app download, first order).
Define the Little Hire: the moment the product is actually brought into the customer's life and used (the dress tag comes off, the app opens again).
Measure the Little Hire, not just the Big Hire; a product that truly solves the job gets hired again and again.
Classic example: many downloaded apps are never reopened — tracking downloads alone tells you nothing about whether the job is being done.
For ecommerce, track repeat purchase and consumption behavior, not just first-order conversion.
caveats: Sales/marketing data commonly reflects only the Big Hire; supplement with consumption data.
Whether a product is 'doing a good job' depends on the customer's ongoing behavior, which single-point data can't show.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map the Four Forces: Push, Pull, Inertia, Anxiety
cards.summary: Two forces drive change (the push of the situation and the pull of the new solution) and two block it (habits of the present and anxiety about the new); all four must be understood.
cards.use_when: You are designing for conversion or adoption and want to reduce friction, not just add appeal.
steps: Identify the push: the frustration or problem substantial enough to trigger action (a merely annoying problem may not qualify).
Identify the pull: how the new solution makes progress that improves the customer's life.
Identify inertia: 'habits of the present' — the comfort of the current workaround, even an imperfect one.

Identify anxiety: fear of the new — cost, learning curve, the unknown. The source cites Kahneman and Tversky that loss aversion is roughly twice as psychologically powerful as the allure of gains (their finding).
Design so the pull clearly exceeds the sum of inertia plus anxiety. Address anxiety explicitly with reassurance.
caveats: Loss aversion 'twice as powerful' is attributed to Kahneman and Tversky, not this book's original claim.
The formula 'pull > inertia + anxiety' is a conceptual model, not a measurable equation.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reduce Switching Anxiety, Not Just Increase Appeal
cards.summary: Innovators over-focus on making the new solution attractive and under-focus on the anxieties that block people from switching.
cards.use_when: You have a strong offer but adoption/checkout is stalling, or you are launching a new or trust-sensitive product type.
steps: Enumerate the customer's specific anxieties: cost, learning something new, fear the new solution fails, fear of needing a backup, fear it's not better.

Design reassurance directly against each: e.g., ING Direct opened physical cafés (you can't do teller cash transactions there) primarily to signal it is a 'real' bank; SNHU's not-for-profit status and real campus reduce fear that online education is a scam.
Remove structural anxiety sources: health clubs using annual contracts reportedly created so much anxiety it prevented people from joining at all.
For ecommerce, translate this into trust signals, easy returns, money-back guarantees, and transparent pricing on the checkout page.
caveats: These are the source's illustrations; the 'annual contracts prevent joining' point is framed as the industry 'coming around to the idea,' i.e., an evolving view.
Reassurance must be credible; a physical café that can't do banking is a brand signal, not a service.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Identify What Must Be Fired for Your Product to Be Hired
cards.summary: Every hire requires firing the current solution — including doing nothing; companies under-consider what their product replaces.
cards.use_when: You are launching or repositioning and need to understand the real competition and switching cost.
steps: List all current solutions for the job, including the solution of doing nothing and any workaround.
Explain how much friction there is in firing each: functional-only solutions are easy to fire, but solutions with emotional and social dimensions are far harder to let go.
Recognize the decision to fire/hire begins long before the customer enters the store or site.

Design messaging and offers that lower the cost of firing: e.g., mobile phones displaced wristwatches; catch-up TV replaced a weekly magazine subscription; anti-incontinence products let people leave home instead of staying in.
caveats: Customers are reluctant to fire anything until sure something is better, even when firing an imperfect solution.
Applies in B2B too — the source notes procurement decisions still carry emotional/social weight (e.g., a plant manager's career anxiety, a project manager's need to look competent).
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Storyboard the Customer's Struggle to Reveal Competing Forces
cards.summary: Sketch the customer's struggle as a narrative (Pixar-style beats) to surface pushes, pulls, anxieties and context.
cards.use_when: You need to convert interview or observation notes into a structured narrative of a decision, or design an onboarding/purchase experience around real moments.
steps: Use the narrative beats: 'Once upon a time... Every day... One day... Because of that we did this... Because of this we did that... Finally I did...'
Talk to consumers as if building a documentary, capturing their struggle to storyboard later.

For each beat, ask about the specific details (who, where, tired or not, how many bags) — Airbnb's founders storyboarded 45 emotional moments for hosts and guests, down to how a guest is greeted on arrival.
Use the storyboard to design moments that match the customer's vision of what they hired you to do — including the first 'Little Hire' moment.
caveats: The Airbnb 45-storyboards detail is a reported example, not a required number.
Storyboarding is a tool to organize the struggle; it is not itself the research.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run a Documentary-Style Job Interview on Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: A JTBD interview reconstructs a timeline of the purchase decision from the first thought, focusing on circumstances, not product features.
cards.use_when: You are interviewing recent buyers/purchasers to understand why they really chose you, and standard feature-preference surveys aren't giving usable answers.
steps: Frame it as filming a documentary: you want all details from when they first started thinking about the purchase, to the decision, to first use.
Reconstruct a timeline with granular, sometimes seemingly irrelevant, probe questions: exact date, weekday/weekend, where, who was with them, what else was in the cart, how they felt.
Do not lead with feature probes ('soft enough? right support? price important?') — the source warns these miss the real story.
Ask about the roles of others in purchase and use, friction points, alternatives considered, and unusual or non-use moments.
Sample size of one: treat each interview as a rich narrative, then cluster stories to find patterns rather than bucketing answers into categories.
caveats: The mattress transcript is explicitly NOT a prototype for all customer-research interviews; it is one illustration of depth.
The ambling, painstaking deficit-gathering is intentional but not suitable as a universal template.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Read the Mattress Case: Clues in Circumstances, Not Features
cards.summary: In the Mattress Agenda interview, the real story was pain, spousal conflict, warranty frustration, and store anxiety — not coil count or firmness.
cards.use_when: You want a concrete model of how an apparently simple, impulse-looking purchase conceals a long, complex job when you gather circumstances.
steps: Note the surface story: Brian Walker bought a $699 memory-foam mattress at Costco on a weekend, seemingly on impulse.

The reconstructed story: it followed four years of back/neck/headaches, a $2,000 pillow-top that sank, a failed Macy's warranty claim (needed 1.5-inch sinkage; a relative sold it to him), spousal sleep conflict, a chaotic Costco trip with kids, and ~3 months of online research.
Extract the job dimension: it was about a good night's sleep and being productive as a business owner, dad, and husband — not coils vs. foam.

Note the firing/anti-anxiety drivers: he feared online/Groupon purchase because of his earlier bad in-store experience; Costco's local presence and easy return lowered that anxiety, and he chose the priciest of two options.
caveats: This is a single retrospective interview; treat as an illustrative pattern, not statistical evidence.
The transcript is edited for length; details may be incomplete.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Watch for Unusual Product Use as a Job Clue
cards.summary: How customers use your product — especially in unexpected or unusual ways — reveals the real job better than their stated preferences.
cards.use_when: You are mining customer behavior or support data and want to spot jobs you aren't currently designing for.
steps: Observe the circumstances in which customers use the product, not just what they say about it.
Flag unusual or unexpected uses and ask what job that behavior is trying to complete.
Look for products used in moments you'd expect them not to be, or not used in moments you'd expect them to be — the source lists both as clue-generating questions.
Cross-check against compensating behavior (see nonconsumer card) to distinguish a true unmet job from noise.
caveats: Unusual use can also indicate misuse or a different segment; investigate before designing for it.
The source frames this as a source of insight, not a proven method with fixed steps.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Your Own Life as a Legitimate Source of Job Insights
cards.summary: The book's takeaways include that personal experience is a valid, rich source of JTBD insights — many successful innovations came from introspection.
cards.use_when: You are stuck for insight or want a low-cost way to start identifying jobs without launching a full research program.
steps: Ask: what are the important, unsatisfied jobs in your own life and the lives of those closest to you?
Flesh out the circumstances and the functional, emotional and social dimensions of the progress you're trying to make.
If you consume your own product, ask which jobs you use it for and where it falls short — and why.

Be mindful of the pitfall the source names: don't start from your existing product and ask how to tweak it (faster? more colors? cheaper?), and don't rely on industry category definitions — you may have already missed the job.
caveats: Personal insight is a starting point; the source still recommends observation of others and nonconsumers.
The trap of only tweaking an existing product is a caution, not a prohibition.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Focus on Cause, Not Luck, in Innovation
cards.summary: The JTBD lens treats innovation as a search for cause — asking what will cause what — so breakthroughs don't depend on lucky accidents.
cards.use_when: You are framing an innovation or experimentation program and want to argue for hypothesis-driven search over hoping for a lucky find.
steps: Explicitly frame the work as discovering what causes a customer to hire your solution in a given circumstance.
Note that the lens lets you look at the same things everyone else sees but 'see differently' — the advantage is in what you look for, not privileged data.
Remember the source's stance: there is no one special method; what matters is the questions you ask and how you piece the resulting information together.
Treat the 'fracking' for jobs metaphor as the mindset: drill deep, then explore widely around a found vein.
caveats: This is the author's framing/opinion, not an empirically proven law.
The book claims no black box, but the cases it cites are selected successes and may suffer survivorship bias.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Signal 'This Is Not for You' to Avoid Alienating Wrong-Fit Buyers
cards.summary: If a customer hires your product for reasons other than its intended job, they may later call it a bad product; signaling who it's not for protects you.
cards.use_when: You have a strong niche offer and are tempted to broaden messaging to grab more buyers, or you're getting mismatched customers who churn or complain.
steps: Identify the job your product is actually solving and what the buyer should expect.
Explicitly signal 'this product is not for you' where the mismatch risk is high, rather than chasing any buyer.
The source's rationale: if a consumer doesn't see their job in your product it's 'game over', and if they hire it for the wrong job and it fails to solve that, they may be alienated permanently.
For ecommerce, translate this into clear product descriptions and expectation-setting to lower returns and bad reviews from mismatched buyers.
caveats: This is the source's opinion and depends on having a defined target job.
Over-signaling can unnecessarily shrink your market; calibrate to where mismatched hires cause real harm.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: B2B Jobs Still Carry Emotional and Social Weight
cards.summary: Even constrained B2B procurement decisions involve anxiety, reputation, career risk and habits of the present.
cards.use_when: You sell to businesses/teams and are tempted to treat the purchase as purely rational or functional.
steps: Identify the personal stakes for the buyer: reputation with peers and managers, being seen as prepared and competent, avoiding sleepless nights or career anxiety.
Design reassurance for the social/emotional job as well as the functional one.

Mercer example: for pension-plan buyouts, clients (HR/CFO) wanted to be seen as careful, competent and having left no stone unturned; Mercer built a Pension Risk Exchange with real-time trading and a modeling/monitoring module so clients could model options before committing — an 'anxiety-reducing practice run.'
Reduce the time and opacity of the process, which the source identifies as core sources of anxiety.
caveats: The Mercer Pension Risk Exchange results (launched in US, UK, Canada; part of growth strategy) are reported case outcomes, not guarantees.
Transfer this reasoning to ecommerce only where you sell to professional buyers who carry personal accountability (e.g., B2B wholesale, team tools).
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reframe 'Good Enough' as a Jobs Question, Not an Opinion
cards.summary: Judgments of whether a product is good enough are unresolvable without a Job to Be Done to anchor them.
cards.use_when: Your team is stuck arguing whether a feature, page, or offer is 'good enough' and the debate keeps cycling.
steps: Stop asking 'Is it good enough?' — the source says this produces opinions and never-ending arguments.
Reframe: 'Is it good enough to help a consumer make this kind of progress in this kind of situation?'
Anchor the answer to the specific circumstance of progress, which the source calls critical to understanding causality.
Use the job definition to make the debate decidable rather than a matter of taste.
caveats: The reframing is attributed to Chris Spiek of the Re-Wired Group, and is presented as his approach/knowledge.
Still requires a well-defined job; without one the reframed question is equally vague.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx
